questions.question_text: Which measure of center is most affected by an extreme outlier?
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so a single extreme outlier pulls it strongly. The median, mode, and quartiles are resistant to outliers.

questions.question_text: If you multiply every value in a dataset by 3, the mean is:
questions.explanation: Multiplying all values by a constant multiplies the mean (and SD) by that constant. Adding a constant would instead shift the mean by that amount.

questions.question_text: In a right-skewed distribution, which ordering is typical?
questions.explanation: Right skew pulls the mean above the median, which is above the mode: mode < median < mean. The mean chases the long right tail.

questions.question_text: A residual is calculated as:
questions.option_b: actual minus predicted (observed y minus ŷ)
questions.explanation: Residual = observed − predicted (y − ŷ). A positive residual means the point lies above the regression line; the sign convention matters.

questions.question_text: If r = -0.9, the relationship is:
questions.explanation: r = -0.9 is close to -1, indicating a strong negative linear relationship. The sign gives direction; the magnitude near 1 gives strength.

questions.question_text: Convenience sampling is problematic because it:
questions.option_b: selects easily accessible individuals, producing a biased, unrepresentative sample
questions.explanation: Convenience samples (whoever is easiest to reach) systematically over- or under-represent groups, biasing results. Random sampling avoids this.

questions.question_text: The three principles of experimental design are control, randomization, and:
questions.explanation: Control (compare to a baseline), randomization (assign treatments by chance), and replication (enough subjects) are the pillars of good experiments. Together they support valid causal conclusions.

questions.question_text: If you draw one card from a standard 52-card deck, P(drawing a heart) is:
questions.explanation: There are 13 hearts out of 52 cards: 13/52 = 1/4. Probability is favorable outcomes over total outcomes.

questions.question_text: For a random variable, if you add a constant c to every value, the standard deviation:
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts the distribution but doesn't change its spread, so the SD is unchanged. Multiplying by c would scale the SD by |c|.

questions.question_text: The standard error of a sample proportion p̂ is:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p̂ is √(p(1−p)/n), which shrinks as n grows. It quantifies the variability of sample proportions.

questions.question_text: If a population is heavily skewed, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal when:
questions.option_d: the population is also normal first
questions.explanation: The Central Limit Theorem makes x̄ approximately normal for large n regardless of population shape. For skewed populations, larger samples are needed.

questions.question_text: A wider confidence interval results from:
questions.option_b: a higher confidence level or smaller sample
questions.explanation: Higher confidence (larger critical value) and smaller samples (larger standard error) both widen the interval. There's a trade-off between confidence and precision.

questions.question_text: If a hypothesis test rejects H₀ at α = 0.05, a 95% confidence interval for the parameter will:
questions.explanation: Rejecting H₀ at α = 0.05 (two-sided) corresponds to the 95% CI excluding the hypothesized value. Tests and intervals are two sides of the same inference.

questions.question_text: A Type I error occurs when you:
questions.option_a: fail to reject a false null
questions.option_b: reject a true null hypothesis (false positive)
questions.explanation: Type I error = rejecting H₀ when it's actually true (a false alarm), with probability α. Type II is failing to reject a false H₀ (a miss).

questions.question_text: The power of a test is the probability of:
questions.option_b: correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: Power = P(rejecting H₀ | H₀ is false) = 1 − β. It measures the test's ability to detect a true effect; it rises with sample size, α, and effect size.

questions.question_text: A chi-square test is used with which type of data?
questions.explanation: Chi-square tests analyze counts in categories (goodness-of-fit, independence, homogeneity). Means use t-tests; relationships between quantitative variables use regression.

questions.question_text: In regression, if the P-value for the slope is 0.001, you conclude:
questions.option_b: strong evidence of a linear relationship between x and y
questions.explanation: A very small P-value (0.001 < 0.05) rejects H₀: β = 0, giving strong evidence of a real linear association. It tests the slope's significance.

questions.question_text: The first quartile (Q1) marks the value below which lie:
questions.explanation: Q1 is the 25th percentile—25% of values fall at or below it. Q2 is the median (50%), Q3 the 75th percentile.

questions.question_text: A scatterplot is used to display:
questions.option_b: the relationship between two quantitative variables
questions.explanation: Scatterplots show how two quantitative variables relate, revealing form, direction, and strength. Pie charts and bar charts handle categorical data.

questions.question_text: Stratified sampling improves on simple random sampling when:
questions.option_b: the population has distinct subgroups you want represented proportionally
questions.explanation: Stratifying ensures each subgroup (stratum) is represented, reducing variability when groups differ. You sample randomly within each stratum.

questions.question_text: The sum of all probabilities in a valid probability distribution equals:
questions.explanation: Probabilities of all possible outcomes must sum to exactly 1, since some outcome is certain to occur. Each must also be between 0 and 1.

questions.question_text: A statistic is to a sample as a parameter is to a:
questions.explanation: Statistics describe samples (x̄, p̂); parameters describe populations (μ, p). Inference uses statistics to estimate unknown parameters.

questions.question_text: Interpreting '95% confident' correctly means:
questions.option_a: 95% of data lie in the interval
questions.option_b: 95% of intervals constructed this way would capture the true parameter
questions.option_c: the parameter has a 95% chance of being random
questions.explanation: Confidence refers to the long-run success rate of the method: 95% of such intervals capture the parameter. The parameter is fixed; intervals vary.

questions.question_text: A two-sided alternative hypothesis is written as:
questions.explanation: A two-sided alternative (μ ≠ value) tests for any difference, splitting α across both tails. One-sided uses > or < for a specific direction.

questions.question_text: A larger chi-square test statistic generally produces a:
questions.option_b: smaller P-value, indicating stronger evidence against the null
questions.explanation: A bigger χ² means observed counts deviate more from expected, yielding a smaller P-value and stronger evidence against H₀ (independence or fit).

questions.question_text: The conditions for regression inference are summarized by the acronym:
questions.explanation: LINE = Linearity, Independence, Normality of residuals, Equal variance—the conditions for valid regression inference. BINS is for binomial settings.

questions.question_text: A boxplot displays which five values?
questions.explanation: A boxplot shows the five-number summary: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. It highlights spread and skewness and flags outliers via the 1.5×IQR rule.

questions.question_text: For independent events, the variance of X + Y equals:
questions.explanation: Variances of independent random variables add for sums (and also for differences). Standard deviations do NOT simply add—you must combine variances first.

questions.question_text: Quadrupling the sample size changes the margin of error by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Margin of error ∝ 1/√n, so quadrupling n halves the margin of error (√4 = 2 in the denominator). Precision improves with the square root of n.
